details:
Project name: Left Behind, Still Talking

Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars

Final project link: https://4o4-team-not-found.vercel.app

Also at: https://left-behind-still-talking.vercel.app (the earlier address; both open the same site)

Demo (7 slides): https://4o4-team-not-found.vercel.app/demo/ (PDF: https://4o4-team-not-found.vercel.app/demo/left-behind-still-talking-demo.pdf)

Audience: students aged 12 to 15

Team: 4O4 Team Not Found

Format: an English website that works on phones and computers, with the keyboard, and offline after the first visit

Summary

Left Behind, Still Talking is a storytelling website in which ten machines that NASA missions left on the Moon and Mars tell their own stories in the first person: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the Apollo laser retroreflectors, the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix and Ingenuity. Each machine explains what it was, why it was sent, how it worked and what it found. Each machine page is a short guided lesson in four steps (the story, how it worked, try it, check what you learned) with points, a "Done" mark for every machine a student finishes, and a printable badge and an ending after all ten. Every machine page has a game that lets students try what that machine did. Animated steps show the engineering behind the science, and a small "Try it" interaction turns one checked number into something students can press or compare. Every fact comes from NASA web pages, and a script checks that each exact quote appears on its saved NASA page.

What we made

- Ten machine pages. Each has a first-person story (250 words or fewer, each with its own opening, shown first as a short version of seven or eight of its own sentences in a chat-like layout, with the whole story one tap away), "How it worked" (five animated steps that change as the reader scrolls, with real NASA photos where they exist), "Try it" (one interaction built on one checked number), "Check what you learned" (three gaps to fill with the story's own checked words, with instant feedback), an "at a glance" strip of key dates, each marked with how many NASA pages it was found on, a fact file of 18 questions in which every answer shows how sure we are, its NASA page and the exact words on that page, and "Even NASA pages sometimes differ" (where NASA pages disagree and what they leave out).

- Start here and plain words. The home page explains in plain words what the site is and what a rover, a lander, a descent stage, a retroreflector and a Mars helicopter are. Hard words carry a short explanation taken from NASA pages (NASA Space Place and Basics of Space Flight), shown when a reader points at or taps the word, and collected on a Glossary page.

- Find a machine and a timeline. On the home page, students can pick a question (such as "Who flew?" or "Who found signs of water?") and see the machines that answer it, each with its own checked story sentence and NASA page, and a timeline of when the ten machines landed or arrived, using the dates in their fact files.

- Games. Surveyor 3: land softly with the engine. Spirit: drive on sunlight and keep out of soft sand. Phoenix: dig with the robotic arm and bring ice to the oven before autumn. Opportunity: brush rocks clean before a dust storm. Lunar Roving Vehicles: steer with the T-stick and drive back before the batteries run out. Sojourner: plan the moves on Earth and send them. Laser retroreflectors: aim a laser at the reflector and catch the light that comes back. Viking 1: pick a smooth site from orbit, then time the parachute and the landing rockets. Eagle descent stage: fill the tanks and the storage space, then land and become the launch pad. Ingenuity: plan the route, then it flies itself to scout for the rover. Each is marked as a simulation and shows no real numbers; next to it, the machine's own checked story sentences tell what really happened, each with its NASA page. They work with mouse, touch and keys.

- Points, ending and badge. Each finished step earns 25 points and each game won 50. Finishing a machine adds it to a printable badge; finishing all ten opens an ending that recalls what each machine said. No name or personal data is asked for or stored; progress stays in the browser.

- Moon: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the Apollo laser retroreflectors (Apollo 11, 14 and 15), the Lunar Roving Vehicles (Apollo 15, 16 and 17).

- Mars: Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, Ingenuity.

- Demo: seven slides at /demo, also available as a PDF.

- Resources page: every NASA page used, every image with its credit and the tools used.

- Design: translucent panels over a space background, drawings with light, shading, surface texture, stars and drifting dust, scroll animations and a soft light that follows the mouse pointer (all turned down for readers who ask for less motion; the pointer light is off on touch screens), picture zoom, keyboard and touch support, works offline after the first visit (the browser keeps a copy of every page and picture).

Impact: who it is for and what a student gains

The site is for students aged 12 to 15. A student learns how each machine worked and what it found, tries one real number, checks what they learned, and can open the NASA page behind every fact. The site has not been tested with students, and we have no usage numbers.

How we checked our facts

- Only NASA web pages (nasa.gov, science.nasa.gov, jpl.nasa.gov, nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov, earth.gsfc.nasa.gov): 55 NASA pages behind the site (the facts, the word explanations, and NASA's and JPL's image-use pages); the same number is shown on the site and in the demo. Pages that refused our connection were opened as Wayback Machine copies, and the site marks them that way.

- Every fact is stored with its page and an exact quote. A script checks that every quote appears, word for word, in the saved page text, and runs after every content change. It was first tested on a known-right quote and a deliberately changed one. On the last build, 834 of 834 quotes were found on their pages.

- Dates and numbers were checked on two NASA pages where two could be found. When pages disagree, the site shows both and does not choose. Values that changed over time carry their year.

- Every story sentence that states a fact is stored with the exact NASA words it rests on, and the script checks that those words are on the page. Every number written in digits in a sentence must also appear in that sentence's own quotes (or in the date of a quoted page). The script does not prove that a sentence means the same as its quote, and it does not check numbers written as words; each fact is shown with its quote so anyone can compare them. NASA's careful words (likely, probably, may) are kept.

- What could not be confirmed is marked "Not found in NASA pages", and the gap is left open.

NASA Data

Every fact, word explanation and photo comes from NASA web pages: NASA Science mission pages, the NSSDCA (NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive) spacecraft and experiment catalog, JPL mission and news pages, NASA History articles, NASA image pages, a NASA Goddard laser-ranging page, NASA Space Place and Basics of Space Flight. In all, 55 NASA pages, listed one by one, per machine, on the site's Resources page (https://4o4-team-not-found.vercel.app/#/resources).

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

No Space Agency Partner data was used. The full list for this field (every NASA page, every image with its credit line, and the tools with their licences) is given in the form's reference fields, generated from the site's own data.

Images

Photos are real NASA images, each with the credit line copied from its NASA page (NASA; NASA/JPL; NASA/JPL-Caltech). Spirit now has two NASA/JPL-Caltech photos (PIA05043 and PIA12312). Phoenix has two images shown on NASA's own Phoenix mission page (science.nasa.gov), with the credit lines copied exactly as that page writes them: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/Texas A&M University, and NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona. The drawings in "How it worked", "Try it" and the games are made by the site's own code. No drawing carries a mark inside the picture; the games carry the label "Game · a simulation, not real data". No NASA logo is used, and NASA does not endorse this project.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) / AI

AI (SI) tools were used to help draft the stories, the drawings and the code. Generated content uses no NASA logo, flag or mission identifier. Images: the photos are NASA images; the drawings in "How it worked", "Try it" and the games are drawn by the site's own code (written with AI help, as stated here) and carry no mark inside the picture, and the games are labeled "Game · a simulation, not real data". Code and data: the use of AI is stated in this descriptive text.

Tools

No outside libraries or web fonts in the site. Build and checks: Python (Python Software Foundation License); screenshots and the demo PDF: Playwright for Python (Apache License 2.0) with Google Chrome.
